bibliographic.title: Personal Health Large Language Models and the Negotiation of Medical Authority in Clinical Care: Opportunities, Risks, and Governance
bibliographic.authors: Wenyi Xie; Jialin Liu; Siru Liu
bibliographic.citation_apa: Xie, W., Liu, J., & Liu, S. (2026). Personal health large language models and the negotiation of medical authority in clinical care: Opportunities, risks, and governance. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 28, e91727. https://doi.org/10.2196/91727

methodology.study_design: conceptual viewpoint with proposed governance framework
methodology.technology_context: Patient-facing or consumer-facing large language model (LLM)-based conversational systems (PH-LLMs) that synthesize user-entered information, patient-generated health data, wearable data, and selected personal health records into personalized, longitudinal, action-oriented health narratives

eligibility.decision_rationale: Viewpoint article explicitly addressing patient-facing PH-LLMs as conversational systems in clinical care, proposing a 3-layer clinical governance framework covering provenance, clinical arbitration, escalation, accountability, privacy, and risk in a regulated health context.

appraisal.notes: Conceptual viewpoint without empirical sample or primary data collection; argument and framework are clearly stated but feasibility, safety impact, and acceptability are deferred to future empirical work.

cerqual.explanation: Highly relevant and internally coherent governance framework for PH-LLMs in clinical care, but confidence is moderated because the article is non-empirical and does not validate the proposed framework.

coding.theme: Clinical governance of patient-facing large language models in care encounters
coding.subtheme: Three-layer framework for patient-brought PH-LLM narratives

synthesis.main_claim: PH-LLMs may shift clinician-patient care from a dyadic to a triadic model of negotiated authority and require a 3-layer clinical governance framework to safely integrate patient-brought algorithmic narratives into routine care.
synthesis.contribution: Proposes a structured 3-layer clinical governance framework (evidence and provenance; clinical arbitration and workflow integration; competence and accountability) for managing risks, privacy, escalation, equity, and accountability when patients bring PH-LLM outputs into clinical encounters.
synthesis.limitations: No empirical evaluation of framework feasibility, documentation burden, equity effects, clinical safety impact, or acceptability; viewpoint relies on conceptual analysis rather than validated implementation evidence.
synthesis.use_in_review: Central conceptual and framework evidence for governance of conversational LLMs in regulated clinical settings, especially patient-initiated PH-LLMs outside institutional oversight.

evidence.claim: Article defines PH-LLMs as patient-facing conversational LLM systems relevant to the review scope.
evidence.excerpt: Personal health large language models (PH-LLMs) are patient-facing conversational systems that synthesize user-entered information, patient-generated health data, wearable data, and selected personal health records

evidence.claim: PH-LLMs operate outside institutional oversight before professional review.
evidence.excerpt: they often originate outside institutional oversight and may be selected, used, or trusted by patients before professional review

evidence.claim: Article addresses governance risks including accountability diffusion and privacy.
evidence.excerpt: privacy and data-governance concerns, diffusion of accountability when harm results from advice produced outside clinical governance

evidence.claim: Authors propose a 3-layer clinical governance framework.
evidence.excerpt: we propose a 3-layer clinical governance framework for patient-brought PH-LLM narratives

evidence.claim: First governance layer covers provenance, uncertainty, and privacy-relevant data use.
evidence.excerpt: The first layer, evidence and provenance, makes AI-generated narratives epistemically legible by clarifying platform identity, data sources, temporal anchoring, uncertainty, and privacy-relevant data-use and retention conditions

evidence.claim: Second governance layer includes risk-stratified intake, documentation, and escalation triggers.
evidence.excerpt: The second layer, clinical arbitration and workflow integration, uses risk-stratified intake, proportionate documentation, escalation triggers, and equity- preserving workflows to embed PH-LLM outputs into routine care

evidence.claim: Third governance layer defines competence, institutional responsibilities, and vendor accountability.
evidence.excerpt: The third layer, competence and accountability, defines the communication competencies, AI literacy supports, institutional responsibilities, vendor accountability, and risk-proportionate verification duties needed for triadic care

evidence.claim: Article frames shift toward triadic negotiated authority in clinical care.
evidence.excerpt: a shift from the traditional dyadic clinician-patient relationship toward a triadic model of negotiated authority, in which clinicians may increasingly need to mediate among clinical evidence, patient values, and algorithmic narratives

evidence.claim: Authors acknowledge need for future empirical validation.
evidence.excerpt: Future empirical work should evaluate its feasibility, documentation burden, equity effects, clinical safety impact, and acceptability among patients, clinicians, and health systems

evidence.claim: Keywords confirm focus on clinical governance and accountability in health LLM context.
evidence.excerpt: Keywords: personal health large language models; clinician-patient relationship; artificial intelligence; medical authority; clinical governance; shared decision-making; patient-generated health data; digital health; accountability
